senses.gloss:
jayantīs
(‘birthdays’)
------------------------------------------
Most of us live in this world in such a way that very soon we are consigned to history. But there are a few, who are the ‘salt of the earth’ who create history! It is but natural for the posterity to remember them with gratitude and pay their homage, especially on their birthdays.
One of the prominent characteristics of the Hindu race is hero-worship, especially if they are religious or spiritual persons. Hence, the number of such birthdays celebrated in our country by the Hindus is legion. Out of that, only a few can be mentioned here since they are, comparatively speaking, a little more known than the others.
First comes the celebration of the जयन्तीस् of the avatāras, especially the दशावतारस्. Since most of the avatāras are mythical personalities and a few of them are of the non-human form, the only data that is available and has to be relied upon, is the one provided by the पुराणस्. The usual dates of these जयन्तीस् are:
1. Matsya — Caitra śukla pañcamī
2. Kūrma — Vaiśākha pūrṇimā
3. Varāha — Bhādrapada śukla tṛtīyā
4. Nṛsiṁha — Vaiśākha śukla caturdaśī
5. Vāmana — Bhādrapada śukla dvādaśī
6. Paraśurāma — Vaiśākha śukla tṛtīyā
7. Śrī Rāma — Caitra śukla navamī
8. Balarāma — Bhādrapada śukla dvitīyā
9. Śrī Kṛṣṇa — Śrāvaṇa कृष्ण aṣṭamī
10. Buddha — Vaiśākha pūrṇimā
or
Kalki — Bhādrapada śukla dvādaśī

From this list, it is seen that परशु-राम jayantī falls on the Akṣayyatṛtīyā day, कूर्म jayantī and बुद्ध jayantī fall on the pūrṇimā of Vaiśākha and that even Kalki—an अवतार yet to come—has been assigned a day of birth.
Kalki seems to have replaced बुद्ध from the list of the दशावतारस् from the 15th century onwards.
The jayantī of परशुराम, the ब्राह्मण warrior who exterminated the wicked kṣattriyas who were abusing their power and tyrannizing the populace, is celebrated in the evening of the अक्षय्य-तृतीया day. Worshipping his image and offering an अर्घ्य (water mixed with sandal paste, दूर्वा grass, flower and rice-grains, to be poured from a शङ्ख or a conch) are important items in the rite.
There are a few temples erected in honour of परशुराम, particularly in the Konkan region of Maharashtra such as the one in Chiplun, where this jayantī is celebrated in a big way.
Though it is sometimes mentioned which of the avatāras has to be worshipped for the fulfillment of which desire, not much material is available on these जयन्तीस्.
Mahāvīra (5th cent. B. C.) jayantī which falls on चैत्र śukla trayodaśī is an important festival day for the Jainas, since he was the last of the Tīrthaṅkaras (originators of जैनिस्म्). It is performed in a solemn way by all the Jainas wherever they are.
Jayantīs of the three ācāryas, शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820), Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137) and Madhva (A. D. 1238-1317), the prominent and pioneering leaders of the three systems of Vedānta (Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita and द्वैत) are celebrated with great éclat by their followers and the maṭhas (monasteries and religious institutions). शङ्कर-jayantī falls on Vaiśākha śukla pañcamī, Rāmānuja-jayantī (more popularly called the tirunakṣatra) on any Vaiśākha śukla पक्ष day associated with the Aridrā or आर्द्रा (Betelgeuse) नक्षत्र and that of Madhva on the विजयदशमी (Āśvayuja śukla daśamī ) day. Apart from a simple worship, devoted study of some of their writings—especially on the प्रस्थानत्रय (Upa-niṣads, Gītā and the Brahmasūtras)—and discourses form part of their observance.
The जयन्तीस् of great religious leaders, especially those who started new religious movements or reform movements are also observed widely among their followers. Mention should be made of Basavaṇṇa or बसवेश्वर (Vaiśākha śukla dvitīyā or tṛtīyā, associated with the नक्षत्र रोहिणी, the fourth group containing five स्तर्स् alpha, theta etc.) who was the top-ranking reformer of his times (12th cent. A. D.) and who was primarily responsible to give a definite shape to the cult of the Liṅgāyats (or वीरशैविस्म्). His jayantī is practically confined to the Karnataka region.
Śrī कृष्ण चैतन्य (A. D. 1485-1533) is another great figure who laid the foundation for Bengal वैष्णविस्म्. His jayantī is observed on the होलि or Dol Pūrṇimā day (Phālguna-pūrṇimā), mostly in Bengal.
The Sikh community celebrates on a grand scale the birthdays of their gurus, especially of गुरु Nānak (A. D. 1469-1539) (Kārttika-pūrṇimā) and गुरु Govind Singh (A. D. 1666-1708) (Mārgaśira कृष्ण caturdaśī).
Sant Tulasīdās (A. D. 1532-1623) of the Rāmcaritmānas fame is another saint highly revered as second वाल्मीकि in the Hindi heartland of North India. His jayantī (Śrāvaṇa śukla saptamī ) is also observed with traditional fervour and devotion.
Tyāgarāja (A. D. 1767-1847) the musician-saint of South India is another highly revered person who is remembered—not on his birthday but on the day of his departure from this world (called puṇyadina or ārādhanā dina)—especially by the musicians and lovers of मुसिच्. A great annual festival is held on that day (Puṣya कृष्ण pañcamī ) at Tiruvayyār in Tamil Nadu, the place where he lived, when all the assembled musicians take part in it by singing a song or two composed by the musician-saint.
Similar is the case of Purandara Dāsa (16th cent. A. D.) another musician-saint, considered as the ड़थेर् of Carnatic मुसिच्. His puṇyadina is observed on पुष्य अमावास्या day. Harikathās (musical discourses based mostly on mythological stories) and singing of his songs are very much a part of the celebration.
Celebration of the birthdays of saints of recent past, like Śrī रामकृष्ण, Śrī Sāradā देवी, Svāmī Vivekānanda, Śrī नारायण गुरु, Śrī रमण महर्षि and Śrī औरोबिन्दो is also gaining ground. This shows that the list of festivals of हिन्दुइस्म् has not yet been completed!
See also JANMĀṢṬAMĪ and RĀMANAVAMĪ.

Jaya
------------------------------------------
Jaya and Vijaya—the twins—are two interesting personalities we come across in the पुराणस् dedicated to the विष्णु cult. They were the children of the sage कर्दम and his wife देवहूति.
Being great devotees of विष्णु, they used to have the vision of Lord विष्णु regularly at the time of worship.
Once they conducted a Vedic sacrifice of the king Marutta admirably well. However, differences arose between them as regards the sharing of the wealth and fees that they had earned. This lead to their mutually cursing each other. जय became an elephant and विजय, a crocodile. They were the two, involved in the story of Gajendramokṣa (See GAJENDRA). After both were liberated from the curses they were taken as dvārapālakas (gate keepers) of वैकुण्ठ, the world of विष्णु.
On another occasion, they rudely prevented the great sages—Sanaka and others—from entering the वैकुण्ठ and were cursed by them. As a result they had to be born as the demons हिरण्याक्ष and हिरण्यकशिपु, रावण and Kumbha-कर्ण, and, शिशुपाल and दन्तवक्र. In all these births, they were killed by Lord विष्णु himself and liberated from the curse. Later they continued their service as the gatekeepers of Lord विष्णु.

Jayadeva
------------------------------------------
One of the most popular Sanskrit poets of all time, whose Gītagovindakāvya has made him immortal in the annals of Indian literature, जयदेव, was born in the village Kendubilva or Kendūli of Bengal as the son of Bhojadeva and Rāmādevī. He is assigned to the 12th century A. D., the exact date being unknown. He was one of the five court-poets of the king Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal.
Though not much is known of him, legends abound in attributing many mira-culous happenings to his life. Some of them are: acceptance of his work, the Gīta-govinda by Lord Jagannātha in preference to the king’s own work; मर्रिअगे with पद्मावती at the behest of Lord कृष्ण; regaining his limbs that had been cut off by robbers, their destruction and redemption on जयदेव’s intervention; death of पद्मावती on hearing the (false) news of जयदेव’s demise and subsequent revival by the Lord’s grace and so on.
Jayadeva’s works are: Gītagovinda, Kārakavāda, Ratimañjarī and Tattvacintā-maṇi.
He is said to have composed a Mahābhārata in Hindi, closely following the original by व्यास.
One more जयदेव (also of the 12th century A. D.), a ब्राह्मण belonging to Vidarbha (in Maharashtra), is also known to the historians of Sanskrit literature. Two works are attributed to him: Prasannarāghava (a drama of seven scenes depicting the story of the Rāmāyaṇa); Candrāloka (a scholarly work on alaṅkāraśāstra or poetics, in ten chapters, comprising 350 stanzas).
The latter work is considered as an authority on poetics. Appayyadīkṣita (16th century A. D.) has written a commentary on it called Kuvalayānanda.

Jayatīrtha
(A. D. 1340-1388)
------------------------------------------
The chief adversary of the Advaita Vedānta of शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) has been the द्वैत Vedānta propounded by Madhva (A. D. 1238-1317). One of the topmost exponents of this system was जयतीर्थ.
His premonastic name was Dhoṇḍūpant. He was born in the small town Maṅgalaveḍe situated on the border of Karnataka and Maharashtra. His ड़थेर् was Raghunātha Rāya of the Deśapāṇḍe lineage. Since the family was rich and also had political patronage, Dhoṇḍūpant grew up as a carefree young man. However, one encounter with Akṣobhyatīrtha, a saṁnyāsin disciple of मध्वाचार्य, changed his life completely. He then and there renounced the world and took to monastic life with the new name जयतीर्थ.
After a course of training under this able teacher, जयतीर्थ gradually excelled him. His works on the द्वैत Vedānta philosophy are:
Nyāyasudhā (a commentary on the Anuvyākhyāna of Madhva, which itself is a commentary on the Brahmasūtras);
Tattvaprakāśikā (a commentary on the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of Madhva);
Nyāyadīpikā (a commentary on the Gītātātparyanirṇaya of Madhva);
Prameyadīpikā (a commentary on the Gītābhāṣya of Madhva).
Jayatīrtha was a contemporary of विद्यारण्य, the well-known teacher and writer on the Advaita philosophy and the founder of the Vijayanagara empire.
He passed away on the bank of the river Kāgiṇī, in Maḷakheḍa (or Mānya-kheṭa).
A cave where he used to compose his works is located near the Yaragoḷa village of Yādgiri taluk (Gulbarga district of Karnataka).

Jayākhya Saṁhitā
------------------------------------------
The Vaiṣṇavāgamas have branched off into two streams: The Pāñcarātra and the Vaikhānasa.
Between these two, the former has produced a voluminous literature—more than two hundred works—and is also being followed in most of the Vaiṣṇava temples, especially in South India.
The three most important treatises of this school are: The Ahirbudhnya Saṁhitā, the Jayākhya Saṁhitā and the Sāttvata Saṁhitā.
The Jayākhya Saṁhitā is a large work of 4592 verses (in the anuṣṭubh metre) spread over 33 paṭalas or chapters. It was perhaps composed between A. D. 300 and 600.
A significant aspect of this treatise is that it gives a detailed account of the philosophy of the Pāñcarātra system. (See PĀÑCARĀTRA ĀGAMAS.)
A very brief summary of its contents may now be given here:
Chapter 1 (166 verses)
This is an introductory chapter and deals with the paratattva or the highest Truth. It starts with the conversation between the sages Saṁvartaka and और्व and later, शाण्डिल्य. The qualifications of the गुरु who is competent to give the spiritual wisdom, as also those of the disciple fit to receive it, are set forth.
Chapter 2 (75 verses)
This chapter deals with Brahmasarga or the च्रेअतिओन् of the four-faced ब्रह्मा from the navel-lotus of Lord विष्णु, च्रेअतिओन् of the world by him, the story of the demons मधु and कैटभ and their being killed by the Lord विष्णु, as also the recovery of the वेदस्.
Chapter 3 (28 verses)
This is a small section dealing with the च्रेअतिओन् from the प्रधान, comprising the three well-known guṇas, and the association of the जीव (the individual सोउल्) with the products of प्रधान.
Chapter 4 (138 verses)
This deals with another aspect of च्रेअतिओन्, viz., Śuddhasarga. It describes how God—called पुरुषोत्तम वासुदेव here—evolves out of himself, three subsidiary forms and some details about them.
Chapter 5 (46 verses)
It is very difficult to know ब्रह्मन् or God. However, the practice of योग and meditation, along with mantrajapa (repetition of the divine name) will be of great help, which, of course, has to be learnt from a competent preceptor. This is the gist of this chapter.
Chapter 6 (250 verses)
This chapter is primarily devoted to the expounding of the mūlamantra (basic मन्त्र of नारायण) along with many other related mantras such as those of लक्ष्मी (spouse of नारायण), Jayā, Māyā, mantras for purifying one’s limbs, mantras of Nṛsiṁha (man-lion इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु) गरुड (eagle-mount of विष्णु or नारायण), कपिल and Varāha (Boar-इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु).
Chapter 7 (124 verses)
This section deals with the mantras of several deities like अनन्त, कूर्म, क्षेत्रपाल, Śrī, गणेश, Matsya, Vāgīśvarī and विष्वक्सेन. These mantras should be formally received from a qualified गुरु and should be kept a secret.
Chapter 8 (117 verses)
This part of the work describes several mudrās (poses of hand) such as जय, शक्ति, हृदय, astra, कपिल and so on. Fifty mudrās have been delineated, as also the results of practising them.
Chapter 9 (71 verses)
This deals exclusively with स्नान or bath, of various kinds including the ones through mantras and ध्यान or meditation.
Chapter 10 (103 verses)
This chapter discusses the topic of समाधि (perfect and total absorption of the मिन्द् on परमात्मन् or God) with all the necessary details like selecting a good spot and preparing a suitable seat, purification of one’s limbs, imagining that the physical body is burnt by the fire-powers of the मन्त्र and entering into a body of light and so on.
Chapter 11 (43 verses)
This small section deals with मन्त्र-न्यास (purification of the body) with appropriate mantras.
Chapter 12 (136 verses)
This chapter deals with mānasayāga or mental worship of Lord विष्णु in detail with all the steps involved in it.
Chapter 13 (236 verses)
As against the internal or mental worship described in the last chapter, this chapter deals with bāhyayāga or external worship.
The various steps detailed here are: drawing the मण्डल (esoteric drawing), establishing the kumbha (pitcher of water), अर्घ्य (water for washing hands), worship of the deity गणेश, meditations on various deities, offering of धूप (incense), ringing of bell, inviting the deity, worship and chanting of hymns.
Chapter 14 (94 verses)
This part of the work is devoted entirely to जप (repetition of the divine name) and the akṣasūtra or जपमाला (rosary), including the methods of preparing it.
Chapter 15 (264 verses)
This section is devoted to agnikārya or होम (offering of oblations into a duly consecrated fire).
The various items of the rite described here are: preparation of the sacrificial pit and alter, method of generating the fire, purificatory processes with regard to the fire including the implements to be used, worship of the fire, various things needed for the होम, offerings into the fire, पूर्णाहुति (final offering), withdrawing the deity worshipped through the fire into oneself, putting out the fire and disposing off the various articles.
Chapter 16 (369 verses)
Various details connected with दीक्षा or initiation are described here.
Some of the important items given in this section are: examining the competence of the disciple, days auspicious for giving दीक्षा, purifying the articles to be used in the ritual of दीक्षा, establishing the कलश (pot filled with water and other materials as prescribed), होम, praying to the deity to be present there, giving a new name to the disciple, some rites connected with the imparting of the मन्त्र, worship of the deity in and through the consecrated fire, worshipping the गुरु by the disciple, and, feeding the ब्राह्मणस् at the end.
Chapter 17 (62 verses)
This short chapter describes the characteristics of the disciple and the गुरु.
Chapter 18 (92 verses)
This section describes the various modes of अभिषेक (consecration by pouring or sprinkling holy water) for a disciple as also for a teacher.
Chapter 19 (36 verses)
How a person duly initiated should practise the disciplines to attain मन्त्र-siddhi (perfection through the repetition of the मन्त्र) is the main topic described here.
Chapter 20 (386 verses)
This is the biggest chapter of the book. Construction and consecration of temples is the main topic discussed in detail. The subjects covered are: methods of preparing oil paintings of deities for worship, icons for worship at home; measurements of a पीठ (pedestal) for icons; doors for temples; time for establishing the images in a temple; rites like अधिवास (‘to live in’), नेत्रोन्मीलन (‘opening of the eyes’) and other related items; पूजा (worship) and rathayātra (procession by temple-car with images); rites for rectifying faults that might have crept in; honouring those who have conducted the rituals and others who have helped; अवभृथ or final ritual bath; what is to be done if there is damage to the image or the pedestal and how to protect the temple and the image in times of political and social turmoil.
Chapter 21 (232 verses)
This chapter deals entirely with pavitrāropaṇa, the act of investiture with the sacred thread, of the images of gods, holy pots (kalaśas), the yāgaśālā (sacrificial shed) and so on. This is said to offset all the defects that may accrue to the religious rites during their performance.
Chapter 22 (80 verses)
This section is dedicated entirely to the description of the characteristics and codes of conduct of the Vaiṣṇavas or devotees of विष्णु. Several varieties of them are delineated here. They are: yatis (saṁnyāsins); ekāntins (those who are deeply devoted to Lord विष्णु and live a lonely life); vaikhānasas (householders wearing the signs of a recluse and living upon what others give); karmasāttvatas (brāhmaṇas who are devoted to God but live by what a king gives for the maintenance of their families); śikhins (brāhma-ṇas performing all their duties but keeping their minds always on Lord विष्णु).
Chapter 23 (155 verses)
This chapter deals with the topic of śrāddha (obsequial ceremonies) in all its details.
Chapter 24 (104 verses)
A topic allied to the previous section, viz., after-death ceremonies, is discussed here.
They are purificatory and other rites for a dead person’s body, preparation of the funeral pyre, च्रेमतिओन्, purificatory bath, collection of bones later on, rules concerning the disposal of the body of a यति (monk), and the rites for a person who dies elsewhere and whose body is not recovered.
Chapter 25 (159 verses)
The various prāyaścittas or expiatory rites for faults and sins—of omission and commission—are described here. Some of the misdeeds mentioned are: not performing the daily rituals like the सन्ध्या-vandana, killing of a ब्राह्मण or a cow, drinking liquor, stealing, eating the ड़ोओद् offered by grave sinners, accepting prohibited gifts, abusing respectable persons, defiling places of worship and so on.
Chapter 26 (133 verses)
This chapter resembles the शाक्त तन्त्रस् in its contents. It deals entirely with the repetition of mantras for fulfilling various worldly desires such as: exorcising the evil spirits, offsetting the evil effects of poisons, attracting or repelling others, causing harm or even death to the enemies, attaining great strength, bringing peace to oneself or others, defeating the army of an enemy and some magical rites.
Chapter 27 (218 verses)
This deals primarily with the sādhanās (spiritual disciplines and associ-ated rites) with the mantras of लक्ष्मी as also of her aspects and associates.
Chapter 28 (157 verses)
This section describes the processes by which certain mantras termed as hṛnmantra (mantra pertaining to the heart), śiromantra (mantra pertaining to the head) and so on, can be realised and the methods of using them to fulfill one’s desires.
Chapter 29 (187 verses)
The topic of mantras and their practice is continued here. The deities dealt with are: Nṛsiṁha, कपिल and Varāha.
Chapter 30 (117 verses)
This too deals with the mantras, but connected with the various implements and jewels of Lord विष्णु like the कौस्तुभ (jewel), vanamāla (garland), शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), गदा (mace), गरुड (eagle-mount) and other related items.
Chapter 31 (49 verses)
This chapter primarily deals with the mantras of the four व्यूहस्: वासुदेव, सङ्कर्षण, प्रद्युम्न and अनिरुद्ध.
Chapter 32 (84 mantras)
As an addenda to the mantras of the deities of the Vaiṣṇava pantheon, this chapter deals with the mantras of Vighneśa (Gaṇapati) and Vāgīśvarī (Sarasvatī) as also of the यन्त्र (mystical diagram) of the letter.
Chapter 33 (87 verses)
This last section of the work describes certain yogic practices as also the signs of approaching death for the योगि.
The work ends with a eulogy of this saṁhitā.
With its detailed treatment of all aspects of the Pāñcarātra system, it has carved for itself an important place. Along with the Ahirbudhnya Saṁhitā, its authority is highly respected in the Vaiṣṇava circles even today.

Jayarāmbāṭī
------------------------------------------
The village जयराम्बाटी is situated in the Bankura district of West Bengal, 117 kms. (73 miles) to the west of the metropolis Calcutta (now Kolkata). It has now become a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे since it is the birth place of Sāradādevī (A. D. 1853-1920), the divine consort of Śrī रामकृष्ण परमहṁस, who is being worshipped as an इन्चर्नतिओन् of God by millions of devotees all over the world.
The chief attraction of the place is the temple dedicated to her, built on the spot where she was born, containing a beautiful marble image of hers. The original shrine was built in A. D. 1923 and expanded later in A. D. 1954, adding a prayer hall as also installing the marble image.
Apart from preserving the old structures associated with her life, the Rama-krishna Math and Mission which is now in charge of the temple, is conducting several rural welfare programmes like running schools and a dispensary.
The following are some of the places the devotee-pilgrims normally visit: the old and the new houses (huts) where Sāradādevī lived; the bathing ghāṭ at the rivulet Āmodar; the temple of goddess Siṁhavāhinī the mud at which place is said to have curative powers: the villages Koalpārā and Sihore.
The Maṭh at Jayarāmabāṭī celebrates the following festivals: birth days of Śrī रामकृष्ण, Sāradādevī and Vivekānanda; दुर्गापूजा (September/October); Jagad-dhātrīpūjā (in November); some of the other festivals of हिन्दुइस्म्.
